lesson.title: Why a Product Equal to Zero Splits Into Two Simple Equations
lesson.summary: The zero product property states that if two factors multiply to zero, at least one of them must be zero, and this single fact turns a factored equation into two easy equations to solve.
lesson.body:
The zero product property says that if a times b equals 0, then a = 0 or b = 0, or both. This might look obvious, but it depends on a special feature of zero: zero is the only number that, when multiplied by anything, always gives zero. For instance, 0 times 5 = 0, 0 times (-217) = 0, and 0 times 0 = 0, no matter how large or small the other factor is. If a and b were both nonzero, their product a times b would also have to be nonzero, since multiplying two nonzero real numbers never produces zero. So the only way the product can equal zero is if at least one of the factors already is zero.

This property matters because it connects the skill of factoring directly to the skill of solving equations. An equation like x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 is hard to solve directly, since there is no single operation that isolates x on one side. But once the left side is factored into (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0, the zero product property applies immediately: since the product of (x - 2) and (x - 3) is zero, one of those factors must itself be zero. That splits one hard equation into two easy ones: x - 2 = 0 or x - 3 = 0, giving x = 2 or x = 3.

To check both solutions, substitute each back into the original equation. For x = 2: 2^2 - 5(2) + 6 = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0. For x = 3: 3^2 - 5(3) + 6 = 9 - 15 + 6 = 0. Both check out, confirming that x = 2 and x = 3 are indeed the two solutions. The same logic extends to more than two factors: if a times b times c = 0, then at least one of a, b, or c must be zero. This is exactly why an equation like x(x - 4)(x + 1) = 0 has three solutions instead of two, x = 0, x = 4, or x = -1, one solution for each factor that is set equal to zero in turn.

There is one condition that must be met before the property can be used: the equation must be set equal to zero, with one side fully factored. It is a common error to try to apply the zero product property to an equation like (x - 2)(x - 3) = 6, setting each factor equal to 6. That does not work, because there are infinitely many pairs of numbers that multiply to 6: 1 and 6, 2 and 3, 12 and 0.5, and many more. The right side must genuinely be zero for the shortcut to apply, since zero is the only number that forces one of its factors to be it.

This property is the bridge between factoring and solving equations more broadly. Where earlier equation-solving relied on inverse operations to isolate a variable on one side of an equation, quadratic and higher-degree equations that factor rely on this different logic: break the product apart, then solve each smaller piece with the same simple reasoning already used for one-step equations. It is the key idea that makes solving by factoring possible in the next stage of the work, and it only works because factoring rewrites an equation as a product in the first place.
